00.cmd: cd esp-labs && uv sync && uv run pio device list
00.goal: Get the toolchain talking to the chip: a data cable, the right USB port, and a serial port name on your Mac.
00.heading: Plug in and find the board
00.note: Flashing says “Failed to connect”? Hold BOOT, tap RST, release BOOT, then flash again.
steps: Plug a data USB-C cable into the port labelled COM (or UART).
Check that a red power LED comes on.
Run the command above. A new /dev/cu.usbmodem… or /dev/cu.wchusbserial… should appear.
Tell Claude the port name and whether your board has one or two USB ports.
00.title: Setup

01.cmd: uv run pio run -d labs/01-hello -e 01-hello -t upload -t monitor
01.goal: Flash your first program. It prints the chip's identity card and cycles the on-board RGB LED through a rainbow.
01.heading: Meet the board
01.note: No colour on the LED? Some boards wire it to GPIO 38. Change PIN_RGB in kit/include/pins.h.
steps: Nothing to wire. Keep the cable in the COM port.
Run the command. Wait for Hard resetting via RTS pin….
Read the identity card: flash should say 16 MB, PSRAM about 8 MB.
Watch the RGB LED next to the chip cycle through colours.
Press Ctrl+C to leave the monitor.
01.title: Hello

02.cmd: uv run pio run -d labs/02-led -e 02-led -t upload -t monitor
02.goal: Build your first circuit and control it by typing commands. The LED keeps animating while the board listens.
02.heading: An LED on the breadboard
02.note: No resistor yet? The code sets the weakest pin drive (about 5 mA) as a safety net. Still add one soon.
steps: Unplug USB before wiring. Seat the board across the breadboard's centre gap.
Wire GPIO 4 → resistor → LED long leg. LED short leg → GND.
Plug back in and run the command. The LED starts breathing.
Type blink 200, sos, level 30, on, off.
02.title: First circuit

03.cmd: uv run pio run -d labs/03-display -e 03-display -t upload -t monitor
03.goal: Drive the ST7789 display over SPI. Draw each frame in PSRAM, then send it in one go so nothing flickers.
03.heading: The 1.9″ IPS screen
03.note: All white or black? Check BLK and RES. Colours inverted? We switch invertDisplay. Garbage? Drop SPI to 20 MHz.
steps: Unplug USB. Wire the 8 display pins as in the table (female-to-male jumpers).
Double-check VCC goes to 3V3, not 5V.
Run the command. You should see red, green and blue bars for 2.5 s.
Then the bench scope: a moving sine wave, uptime and frames per second.
Tell Claude the fps from the monitor and anything that looks off.
03.title: Display

variants.cmd: uv run pio run -d labs/03b-showcase -e 03b-showcase -t upload
variants.goal: Same wiring as lesson 03. Four scenes show what the S3 can draw: real-time 3D, per-pixel effects, particles and a live dashboard of your chip. The on-board BOOT button switches scenes.
variants.label: Variation 1 · BOOT button
variants.note: BOOT only matters at power-on. Don't hold it while pressing RST or plugging in, or the chip waits in flash mode. If that happens, just press RST.
steps: Keep the display wired exactly as in lesson 03. Nothing new to plug in.
Flash with the command above (or tell Claude “go” and it runs it for you).
Watch the 3D torus, then press BOOT to step through Plasma, Fireworks and the Dashboard.
Long-press BOOT (0.6 s) to stop or restart the 12-second auto-cycle.
Open uv run pio device monitor and type scene 2, hud, auto off.
Note fps, draw ms and send ms for each scene and tell Claude. They feed the speed lesson.

variants.cmd: uv run pio run -d labs/03b-showcase -e 03b-showcase-button -t upload
variants.goal: The same four scenes, now driven by your own push button on GPIO 5: click, double-click, long press. The screen is an output on 8 wires; the button is an input on 2. This variation shows both together.
variants.label: Variation 2 · Push button
variants.note: Never reacts? Check the signal wire really ends on 5, not its neighbour 4, and that both wires end on the ESP32, not on breadboard holes. Always “pressed”? Use diagonally opposite legs.

panels.title: Wiring on the ESP32: screen + button

steps: Unplug USB. Keep the display wired exactly as in lesson 03.
Push the button into the breadboard so it straddles the centre gap, away from the board.

Jumper from leg A to the ESP32's pin 5. On an expansion board that is the socket labelled 5, two past the display's BLK wire on 7. Jumper from the diagonal leg D to any GND. Breadboard holes are not connected to the ESP32, so both wires must end on the ESP32's own sockets.
Plug in and flash with the command above (or tell Claude “go”).
Press the button: click = next scene, double-click = previous, long press = auto-cycle on/off. BOOT does the same.
Open uv run pio device monitor: every click logs how many contact bounces it filtered.

B1.cmd: uv run pio run -d labs/ble-lab-b1 -e ble-lab-b1 -t upload

commands.command: uv run pio run -d labs/ble-lab-b1 -e ble-lab-b1 -t upload
commands.does: Builds lab B1 and writes it to the board. The first build downloads NimBLE-Arduino 2.5.1 (the Bluetooth stack).
commands.fix: “Failed to connect”: hold BOOT, tap RST, release BOOT, run it again.
commands.see: Hard resetting via RTS pin…. The screen shows the radar with a sweeping line.

commands.does: Opens the serial monitor (the board restarts).
commands.fix: No NimBLE … up line: the stack didn't start; unplug and replug the board.
commands.see: ble-lab-b1: NimBLE 2.5.1 up, address …, + active scan, 100/100 ms (100% listening), then the command list.

commands.does: Prints every device heard in the last 30 s, strongest first: RSSI, a distance guess, kind, address and its type, packets, name or maker.
commands.fix: Empty: is Bluetooth on around you? Phones often advertise only when their screen is on or an app wants them to.
commands.see: A table such as 1 -46 0.6 phone 5A:3C:… private (RPA) 412 Apple. Ten to fifty rows in a flat, fewer in a house.

commands.command: (hold your phone next to the board)
commands.does: Your phone becomes the strongest device. Unlock it: iPhones advertise more often with the screen on.
commands.fix: Android phones may stay silent: open nRF Connect and use its Advertiser tab, or switch on Nearby Share / Quick Share for a moment.
commands.see: On the radar, one blip moves to the centre; on list it jumps to row 1 with about −40 dBm.

commands.does: Picks row 1 for the inspect view and prints its advertisement and scan response, structure by structure.
commands.fix: no scan response: some devices don't send one; in passive mode nobody asks for it.
commands.see: [02 01 | 1A] Flags, [0A FF | 4C 00 10 …] Manufacturer data (Apple: Nearby info), maybe [02 0A | 0C] TX power.

commands.does: Prints one line per packet of the picked device, with the time since the previous one.
commands.fix: watch off stops it. Too many lines: near -60 first.
commands.see: < + 182 ms -47 dBm 31 B lines. Some gaps are missed packets (your phone sent it on a channel the board wasn't listening on); the shortest repeating gap is its interval.

commands.does: Passive: the board only listens. Active: it also sends a scan request to every scannable device and gets a second packet back, the scan response.
commands.see: In passive mode the inspect view loses its scan rsp row and some names turn into makers. The air view shows the mode.

commands.does: Listen 30 ms out of every 100 (30 % duty cycle) instead of all the time.
commands.fix: Window must be ≤ interval.
commands.see: Packets per second on the air view drop to about a third. Phones scan like this to save battery. timing 100 100 goes back.

commands.does: Takes the picked device's average RSSI as the 1 m reference for the distance guesses.
commands.fix: Distances jump by ±1 m: that's RSSI. Bodies, walls and the phone's orientation move it by 5–10 dB.
commands.see: + 1 m = -58 dBm now: distances use it. Walk away: the blip drifts outwards.

B1.goal: Phones, watches, earbuds, speakers, keyboards and beacons announce themselves all day: short advertising packets on three radio channels, many times a second, whether anyone listens or not. B1 turns the board into a listener. It draws them on a radar, guesses what each one is, and takes a packet apart byte by byte. The radio uses NimBLE, a lightweight Bluetooth stack; the firmware is its own (ble-lab-b1), with shared code in kit/lib/ble-kit.
goalCheck: The radar view shows blips and the monitor's list prints a table of devices with a kind (phone, audio, keyboard…).
You picked your own phone (bring it close: it becomes the strongest) and bytes shows its AD structures: Flags, then manufacturer data (Apple, Samsung, Google…).
watch prints one line per packet of your phone, and you can read its advertising interval from the +… ms gaps.
Switching mode passive makes the scan responses (and some names) disappear; mode active brings them back.
B1.goalLine: Find your own phone among the devices around you, read its packets byte by byte, and measure how often it advertises.
B1.heading: Hear every Bluetooth device around you
B1.note: Everything here is what devices broadcast to anyone; the board never connects to them. Still, the list is your neighbours' gadgets: don't post their addresses (they stay out of the committed logs). Phones change their private address about every 15 minutes, so the same phone can show up twice. Distances are guesses from signal strength, good to a factor of two. The ESP32-S3 has Bluetooth LE only: Classic Bluetooth (most audio streaming, older keyboards) is invisible to it.

panels.intro: Eight labs, each its own firmware. The board starts as a pure listener and ends up hosting your keyboard. Pick a lab to see the board's role and which way the data flows; the lock marks the labs where pairing and encryption matter.
panels.title: The Bluetooth track, from listening to hosting

panels.intro: Bluetooth LE splits the 2.4 GHz band into 40 channels of 2 MHz. Advertising uses only three of them, 37, 38 and 39, placed in the gaps between the usual Wi-Fi channels 1, 6 and 11. Every advertising event sends the same packet on all three, one after the other. The scanner listens on one channel at a time: a packet counts only if it lands inside a listening window on its channel. Move the window slider and watch how many packets the board catches; switch to active to see the scan request and response.
panels.title: Three channels, many shouts

panels.intro: What a radio actually sends, from the first bit to the checksum. Pick a device, then step through the fields with ◀ ▶. The AD structures in the middle are exactly what the inspect view and the bytes command show.
panels.title: One advertising packet, byte by byte

panels.intro: Four views. A click on the push button (or BOOT) goes to the next one, a double-click runs the action written at the bottom left, a long press pauses or resumes the scan. The icon at the top right is the radio: a sweeping radar while it scans.
panels.title: What the screen shows

steps: Keep the screen wired as in lesson 03 (push button optional). Flash ble-lab-b1 and open the monitor. Checkpoint 1: NimBLE 2.5.1 up and the radar sweeping.
Type list. Checkpoint 2: a table of devices with kinds; look for audio (your JBL advertises for its app), keyboard/mouse and Apple or Microsoft makers.
Hold your unlocked phone next to the board, pick 1, click to inspect. Checkpoint 3: its bytes in coloured AD structures, the address type is private (RPA).
Type watch for ten seconds, then watch off. Checkpoint 4: you can name your phone's advertising interval.
Try mode passive / mode active and timing 100 30 / timing 100 100 while looking at the air view.
Optional: calib with the phone 1 m away, then walk to the other side of the room and watch the radar.
B1.title: Listen

B2.cmd: uv run pio run -d labs/ble-lab-b2 -e ble-lab-b2 -t upload

commands.command: uv run pio run -d labs/ble-lab-b2 -e ble-lab-b2 -t upload
commands.does: Builds lab B2 and writes it to the board.
commands.fix: “Failed to connect”: hold BOOT, tap RST, release BOOT, run it again.
commands.see: The packet view: bench ADV_IND every 100 ms and two rows of coloured cells.

commands.does: Opens the serial monitor.
commands.see: + bench ADV_IND every 100 ms, 24+7 B and the command list.

commands.command: nRF Connect → Scanner → Bench B2 (tap the row, don't connect)
commands.does: The phone is the scanner now (one board can't hear itself). Tapping the row opens the advertisement's details.
commands.fix: Not listed: pull down to refresh; adv on. On iPhone, Manufacturer data shows as one hex string: the same bytes.
commands.see: Complete Local Name Bench B2, Manufacturer data 0xFFFF 0x01…; the last two bytes (uptime) change every second. Tap RAW to see all 24 bytes.

commands.does: Counts a press into the packet. The board replaces the advertisement data; the controller sends the new bytes from the next event on.
commands.see: - presses 1: in the next packet; on the packet view two cells flash white; in nRF Connect byte 4-5 of the manufacturer data becomes 01 00.

commands.does: Prints both packets structure by structure.
commands.see: [02 01 | 06] Flags, [09 09 | 42 65 6E 63 68 20 42 32] Name, [0A FF | FF FF 01 01 00 2E 10 2C 01] Manufacturer data.

commands.does: Apple's layout: 4C 00 02 15, a 16-byte UUID, major, minor, the power at 1 m. 30 of 31 bytes: the name moves to the scan response.
commands.fix: iPhone shows nothing special, or not the beacon: iOS filters iBeacon frames out of every app's scan. Only Core Location (region monitoring) sees them.
commands.see: + ibeacon ADV_IND every 100 ms, 30+10 B. Android nRF Connect: “iBeacon”, UUID BA5E0000-B1E5-…, Major 1, Minor 2. B1 on another board would show the beacon kind in violet.

commands.does: Eddystone-URL: service data FEAA with a compressed URL (https:// = 1 byte, .com/ = 1 byte).
commands.fix: Android used to pop these up as notifications (Physical Web); that's gone since 2018. Apps still decode them.
commands.see: nRF Connect shows Eddystone URL https://github.com/. A URL too long: x the URL doesn't fit…, and the old one stays.

commands.does: First ADV_SCAN_IND (may be scanned, not connected), then ADV_NONCONN_IND: a pure broadcast that answers nobody.
commands.fix: interval raised to 100 ms: the floor for non-connectable adverts (Bluetooth 4.x rule; 5.0 allows 20, beacons stay at 100+).
commands.see: The packet view's title changes; nRF Connect's Connect button disappears; the scan response row empties.

commands.does: How often the board shouts. Click to the air and budget views for each.
commands.fix: interval 20 refused with connectable off: switch connectable on first.
commands.see: + … every 1000 ms; nRF Connect's interval column (Android) or the RSSI graph updates slower; the budget's coin-cell life jumps from weeks to years.

commands.does: TX power in dBm (the shell's built-in command). Lower = shorter range and less current.
commands.see: nRF Connect's RSSI drops by about 20 dB at the same distance; the name mode's TX power field changes too.

commands.does: Stops advertising. The board is invisible.
commands.see: - advertising off: the board is invisible; nRF Connect greys it out after a few seconds.

B2.goal: In B1 the board listened. Now it becomes a beacon: it packs live values (button presses, the chip's temperature, uptime) into its own 31-byte advertisement, so any phone nearby can read them without connecting. The same budget then carries an iBeacon, an Eddystone-URL or just a name. You choose how often it shouts (the interval) and how loud (TX power), and see what that would cost a coin-cell beacon.
goalCheck: nRF Connect lists Bench B2 and shows Manufacturer data 0xFFFF whose bytes change every second (the uptime) and when you double-click (the presses).
The packet view shows 24 of 31 bytes in coloured structures, and the changing bytes flash white.
mode ibeacon shows up as an iBeacon on Android (on iPhone apps can't see iBeacons: that's iOS, not you), mode url as an Eddystone URL in nRF Connect.
With connectable off and scanresp off the packet view says ADV_NONCONN_IND, nRF Connect no longer offers Connect, and the interval can't go below 100 ms.
You can explain from the budget view why beacons advertise every 500-1000 ms and not every 20.
B2.goalLine: Make the board broadcast live values that your phone reads without ever connecting.
B2.heading: The board shouts its own data
B2.note: Anyone nearby can read what the board broadcasts: never put anything private in an advertisement. 0xFFFF is the company ID the Bluetooth SIG reserves for tests, fine on a bench, not for a product. iPhone apps can't see iBeacon frames at all (iOS removes them from scans), so test that mode on Android or with B1 on a second board. The budget view is an estimate for a typical coin-cell beacon chip with its stated assumptions: this ESP32-S3 board itself draws about 80 mA with the screen on, far too much for a coin cell. The one radio can't hear itself, so the phone is the scanner in this lab.

panels.intro: Every field you add costs its data plus 2 bytes (length and type). Put each one in the advertisement, in the scan response (sent only when a scanner asks), or leave it out, and watch the 31-byte budget fill. The board's four modes are presets.
panels.title: Build an advertisement

panels.intro: The board sends each advertising event on channels 37, 38 and 39 in a row, every interval plus a random 0-10 ms. A phone listens on one channel at a time, for a window out of each scan interval. Slide the numbers and count what gets caught. Switch the random delay off to see why it exists.
panels.title: When does a scanner hear it?

panels.intro: Four views. A click goes to the next one; a double-click anywhere counts a press into the packet; a long press switches advertising on or off.
panels.title: What the screen shows

steps: Same wiring as B1. Flash ble-lab-b2 and open the monitor. Checkpoint 1: bench ADV_IND every 100 ms, 24+7 B.
Install nRF Connect (or LightBlue) on your phone and find Bench B2; tap it open, don't connect. Checkpoint 2: Manufacturer data 0xFFFF with bytes that change every second.
Double-click the board's button a few times. Checkpoint 3: the press counter changes on the phone without any connection.
Try mode ibeacon (Android shows it) and mode url. Compare with the builder above: which fields moved to the scan response, and why?
connectable off, scanresp off. Checkpoint 4: ADV_NONCONN_IND, no Connect button on the phone.
Click to air and budget, then try interval 1000 and power -12. Checkpoint 5: you can say what each costs and what it buys.
B2.title: Be seen

B3.cmd: uv run pio run -d labs/ble-lab-b3 -e ble-lab-b3 -t upload

commands.command: uv run pio run -d labs/ble-lab-b3 -e ble-lab-b3 -t upload
commands.does: Builds lab B3 and writes it to the board.
commands.fix: “Failed to connect”: hold BOOT, tap RST, release BOOT, run it again.
commands.see: The gatt view with five rows; the radio icon shows rings: advertising.

commands.does: Opens the serial monitor.
commands.see: - advertising as "Bench B3", then the command list.

commands.command: nRF Connect → Scanner → Bench B3 → Connect
commands.does: Your phone connects. Install nRF Connect for Mobile (Nordic, free; iPhone and Android) or LightBlue. On iPhone, never connect from Settings → Bluetooth: apps do it.
commands.fix: Bench B3 not listed: scroll, or filter by name “Bench”. Still nothing: adv on.
commands.see: Monitor: + connected: 5A:3C:… and - interval 30.00 ms …, soon - MTU 255: 252 bytes of data per packet. The radio icon turns into two rings, the LED steady blue.

commands.does: Writes 3 bytes: red FF, green 50, blue 00.
commands.fix: LED wants 3 bytes, got 1: choose Byte Array, not Text or UINT8.
commands.see: < write LED FF 50 00; the on-board LED glows orange; the LED row flashes blue and shows the colour swatch.

commands.does: Writes UTF-8 text (up to 40 bytes).
commands.fix: Accents show as boxes: the screen font is plain ASCII.
commands.see: < write Message "hello bench"; click to the message view: big text, “written 3s ago”.

commands.command: Button → subscribe (the ↓↓↓ / bell icon), then click the board's button
commands.does: Subscribing writes 01 00 into the Button's CCCD. Each gesture then pushes a 3-byte value: gesture, count (2 bytes).
commands.fix: (nobody subscribed) in the monitor: subscribe first.
commands.see: < subscribe Button (CCCD = 1), then per click > notify Button: click #3; the phone shows 01-03-00. A bell appears on the Button row.

commands.does: Reads 2 bytes (°C × 100, little-endian). The 2904 descriptor tells apps how to show it.
commands.see: nRF Connect shows 41.42 °C (raw 2E-10); subscribed, it updates every 2 s.

commands.does: Asks the phone for a 100-200 ms interval (and to let the board skip 4 events), then for 15-30 ms. The phone decides.
commands.fix: params rejected or ignored: iPhones refuse some values; try again after a few seconds.
commands.see: - new params: 112.50 ms, latency 4; the dot on the link view slows down. Notifications now arrive in bursts.

commands.does: Hangs up. The board advertises again by itself.
commands.see: ! disconnected 0x16: we hung up; the link view keeps the reason.

B3.goal: Advertising is shouting; a connection is a private conversation. The phone (the central) connects to the board (the peripheral), and from then on they meet on a fixed beat, the connection interval, hopping over 37 data channels. On the board sits a small database, the GATT table: the Bench service with LED, Message, Button, Temperature and Uptime. From nRF Connect or LightBlue you write the LED's colour, put a message on the screen, read the chip's temperature and subscribe to the button.
goalCheck: nRF Connect (or LightBlue) shows Bench B3, connects, and lists the Bench service with five named characteristics plus Device Information and Battery.
Writing FF5000 to LED turns the on-board LED orange, and the LED row flashes blue on the gatt view.
Writing text to Message shows it big on the message view.
After you subscribe to Button, every click on the board arrives on the phone as a notification; the Temperature notifies every 2 s.
The link view shows the connection interval, MTU and RSSI, and params slow visibly changes the interval.
B3.goalLine: Control the board from your phone over Bluetooth, and see every operation arrive on the gatt view.
B3.heading: Your phone connects, reads and writes
B3.note: Anyone nearby can connect to Bench B3 and change the LED: there is no pairing yet, everything travels in plain text. That's B4. iPhones cache a device's GATT table: if a later lab changes the table and the iPhone shows old rows, turn Bluetooth off and on. The ESP32-S3 has one radio: B3 doesn't use Wi-Fi, so there is no coexistence to worry about.

panels.intro: What happens when you tap Connect in nRF Connect, and when you write the LED or the board notifies a click. Each step shows the real ATT bytes: the first byte is the opcode, the next two the handle (the row number in the board's table), the rest the value.
panels.title: From advert to conversation, step by step

panels.intro: The board's GATT table as nRF Connect shows it. Press an operation to send it: the packet crosses over, the board's row lights like on the gatt view, and the bytes are decoded underneath.
panels.title: The Bench service, live

panels.intro: Four views. A click goes to the next view; every gesture (click, double-click, long press) is also sent to a subscribed phone as a Button notification. A double-click on the gatt and message views sends an extra click.
panels.title: What the screen shows

steps: Same wiring as B1. Flash ble-lab-b3, open the monitor. Checkpoint 1: advertising as "Bench B3".

On your phone, install nRF Connect (or LightBlue), find Bench B3 and connect. Checkpoint 2: connected in the monitor and the Bench service with LED, Message, Button, Temperature and Uptime on the phone.
Write FF5000 to LED and a text to Message. Checkpoint 3: the LED is orange, the message is on the screen.
Subscribe to Button and Temperature, then click the board's button. Checkpoint 4: the values arrive on the phone; bells on the gatt view.
Click to the link view and try params slow / params fast and phy 2m. Checkpoint 5: the interval changes on screen.
Type led auto to give the LED back to the radio status, then disconnect.
B3.title: Connect & talk

B4.cmd: uv run pio run -d labs/ble-lab-b4 -e ble-lab-b4 -t upload

commands.command: uv run pio run -d labs/ble-lab-b4 -e ble-lab-b4 -t upload
commands.does: Builds lab B4 and writes it to the board.
commands.fix: “Failed to connect”: hold BOOT, tap RST, release BOOT, run it again.
commands.see: The ceremony view: “Waiting for a phone to connect...” and eight grey phases.

commands.does: Opens the serial monitor.
commands.see: - pairing: Passkey · lock off · anyone may connect, then the command list. The method is saved in flash: it survives a reflash of B4.

commands.command: nRF Connect → Bench B4 → Connect → Vault → read
commands.does: The Vault refuses a plain-text link with “Insufficient Authentication”; the phone reacts by starting pairing.
commands.fix: No prompt on iPhone: read the Vault again. On Android the prompt may be a notification.
commands.see: The phone asks for a code; the TFT shows PASSKEY ENTRY and six digits; the monitor ! passkey 482915: type it on the other device. The ceremony view's phases 1-5 fill, “check” pulses amber.

commands.command: type the six digits on the phone
commands.does: Both sides check the passkey bit by bit (20 rounds of confirm and random values), then encrypt and swap keys.
commands.fix: x … confirm failed: wrong passkey: a typo. Read the Vault again for a new code.
commands.see: + secured: authenticated, bonded, key 16 B, - identity: 4C:…; the phone reads the bench's secret: 42. Lock and key icons in the header; the ceremony track is complete.

commands.command: disconnect, then connect again and read the Vault
commands.does: A bonded phone has the keys: no ceremony, encryption starts straight away.
commands.see: The ceremony view says stored keys: bonded before, no ceremony and jumps from connect to encrypted.

commands.does: Lists the bonded devices by identity address (the IRK resolves the phone's private address to it).
commands.see: 1 bonded device … and 1 4C:… random static (iPhones and most Androids use a random static identity). The bonds view marks it “<- here”.

commands.command: forget all, then forget Bench B4 on the phone
commands.does: Deletes the bonds on the board. The phone still has its half: forget the device in Settings → Bluetooth (iPhone: ⓘ → Forget This Device; Android: the gear → Unpair; macOS: right-click → Forget).
commands.see: ! forgot every bond, - now forget "Bench B4" on the phone too. If you skip the phone part: x ENC_CHANGE failed 0x206: key missing: one side forgot the bond.

commands.command: pair justworks, then read the Vault
commands.does: The board now says “no input, no output”: nobody can check anything. The link gets encrypted, but not authenticated.
commands.fix: That's the lesson: Just Works stops eavesdroppers, not a man in the middle.
commands.see: + secured: Just Works, bonded, a violet lock, but the Vault read fails again with Insufficient Authentication: the Vault demands MITM protection.

commands.command: pair compare (forget first), read the Vault, then click
commands.does: Both screens show the same six digits. A click on the board says yes, a long press no; the phone has its own button.
commands.fix: A long press (no) ends with numbers didn't match: said no.
commands.see: NUMERIC COMPARISON on the TFT, the same number on the phone; after both yes: + secured: authenticated, bonded.

commands.does: Only bonded identities go on the filter accept list; the controller resolves each private address with the stored IRKs and refuses the rest.
commands.fix: Locked yourself out: allow anyone over serial.
commands.see: + only bonded phones may connect (saved). Your phone connects; another one (or yours after forgetting) gets no connection at all.

commands.does: LED and Message also need an encrypted link. Permissions are part of the GATT table, built once at start-up, so the board saves the setting and restarts.
commands.fix: iPhone shows old permissions: turn Bluetooth off and on (it caches the table).
commands.see: lock on saved. … the board restarts now...; afterwards writing the LED from a non-paired phone triggers pairing too.

B4.goal: In B3 anyone nearby could connect and read every byte. B4 adds a Vault characteristic that the board only serves over an encrypted, authenticated link. Touch it from the phone and pairing starts: the passkey appears big on the TFT, or both screens show the same six digits and you confirm with the button. Afterwards the board bonds: it keeps the keys in flash, recognises your phone behind its changing private address, and can refuse everyone else.
goalCheck: With pair passkey, reading the Vault on the phone brings up a code prompt, the TFT shows six digits, and after typing them the phone reads the bench's secret: 42.
The ceremony view fills phase by phase up to bonded, and the header shows a violet lock and an amber key.
With pair justworks (after forget all and forgetting the board on the phone) the link is encrypted but the Vault is still refused: you can explain why.
With pair compare you accept the matching numbers with a click on the board and a tap on the phone.
After allow bonded, your phone still connects, and a second phone (or the same phone after forgetting the board) can't.
B4.goalLine: Pair your phone with each of the three methods, read the Vault, and lock the board to your phone.
B4.heading: Make the link private, and remember who's allowed
B4.note: Pairing has two halves: whenever you forget on the board, forget the board on the phone too (iPhone: Settings → Bluetooth → ⓘ → Forget This Device; Android: Bluetooth → gear → Unpair; macOS: System Settings → Bluetooth → right-click → Forget), or the next connection fails with “key missing”. If only the phone forgot, NimBLE accepts the new pairing and replaces the old bond by itself (repeat pairing). The method, lock and allow settings are saved in flash (namespace b4) and survive restarts. NimBLE doesn't report the features, method and key-exchange phases one by one: the ceremony view draws them as inferred (a ring) once a later phase proves they happened. The board ships with the secret “the bench's secret: 42”; vault <text> changes it until the next restart.

panels.intro: At the start of pairing each side says what it can do: show a number, type one, press yes or no, or nothing at all. The two answers decide the method. Pick the phone's and the board's capabilities (the board's are what pair sets) and see who shows and who types.
panels.title: Which pairing method? It depends on both sides

panels.intro: The Security Manager Protocol (SMP) messages that cross the air when the phone reads the Vault, with their real bytes. Each method differs only in the middle: how a person proves nobody sits in between.
panels.title: One pairing, packet by packet

panels.intro: Five views. A click goes to the next one; a double-click runs the action in the footer (secure, bonds, press). While numbers wait for comparison, the button answers instead: click = yes, long press = no.
panels.title: What the screen shows

steps: Same wiring as B3. Flash ble-lab-b4 and open the monitor. Checkpoint 1: pairing: Passkey in the start-up lines.
Connect from nRF Connect and read the Vault. Type the six digits from the TFT. Checkpoint 2: the phone reads the secret; the ceremony view is complete; lock and key in the header.
Disconnect and reconnect. Checkpoint 3: “stored keys”: no passkey this time.
forget all and forget the board on the phone. pair justworks, read the Vault. Checkpoint 4: encrypted, yet refused. Why?
Forget on both sides again, pair compare, read the Vault and click to confirm. Checkpoint 5: authenticated and bonded.
allow bonded. Checkpoint 6: your phone connects; after forgetting it on the phone, it can't. Finish with allow anyone.
B4.title: Pair & trust

B5.cmd: uv run pio run -d labs/ble-lab-b5 -e ble-lab-b5 -t upload

commands.command: uv run pio run -d labs/ble-lab-b5 -e ble-lab-b5 -t upload
commands.does: Builds lab B5 and writes it to the board.
commands.fix: “Failed to connect”: hold BOOT, tap RST, release BOOT, run it again.
commands.see: The sketch view: “Open the ble-app, connect”. The radio icon shows rings: advertising as Bench B5.

commands.command: cd esp-labs/apps/ble-app && pnpm install && pnpm dev
commands.does: Installs the app once (React, Vite, TypeScript, exact versions) and serves it at http://localhost:5177. No server code: Vite only hands the page to the browser.
commands.fix: Port busy: another lab's app runs; stop it or pnpm dev --port 5178.
commands.see: ➜ Local: http://localhost:5177/

commands.does: The browser's own device chooser opens (a page can never connect by itself). It lists boards with the Bench service, names starting with “Bench”, or BLE-MIDI instruments.
commands.fix: “Web Bluetooth isn't available here”: use Chrome or Edge, and localhost (not 127.0.0.1 or the Mac's IP).
commands.see: Pick Bench B5. The Connect tab shows the GATT explorer; the monitor prints + connected: …. The first time, macOS asks to allow Chrome to use Bluetooth.

commands.command: Control tab: drag the colour wheel, send a message
commands.does: Each move writes 3 bytes to LED (throttled to one write per 80 ms); Send writes up to 40 bytes of UTF-8 to Message.
commands.fix: LED stays put after led auto: move the wheel again, the board claims the LED back.
commands.see: The LED follows your finger; < write LED 1F 5C 99 lines in the monitor and blue packets crossing the app's air strip.

commands.does: Strokes go to Canvas (ba5e0010) as writes without response: 02 cc cc w n + 3 bytes per point, every 50 ms. The board queues them in the NimBLE task and draws them in loop().
commands.fix: DROPPED on the board: you drew faster than 16 queued writes; nothing breaks, a few strokes are missing. sketch: a command was cut off: the app fell back to 20-byte writes (MTU 23).
commands.see: The same lines on the board's sketch view; at the bottom 412 cmds 96 writes 9120 B.

commands.command: Live tab (then touch the wire on GPIO 1)
commands.does: Subscribes to Sensors: 12 bytes every 200 ms (temperature, touch, free heap, RSSI, a sequence number).
commands.fix: Touch line flat: GPIO 1 has no wire; any jumper works, the bare metal end is the sensor.
commands.see: Four moving lines in the app and the same four sparklines on the board's live view; “notifying the app: 230 sent”. Touching the wire's free end makes the touch value jump by thousands.

commands.does: Subscribes to Speed and writes 01 50 C3 00 00. A small task on the board notifies 50,000 bytes in (MTU − 3)-byte packets until the stack's buffers are full, waits, and continues; then a 15-byte summary.
commands.fix: speed: subscribe to Speed (ba5e0012) first: open the Speed tab once before running from serial.
commands.see: Monitor: < write Speed: start 50000 bytes then + speed: 50000 B in 2310 ms = 21.6 kB/s. The app shows a bar with the same order of magnitude.

commands.command: Speed tab: Fast interval, 2M PHY, Long packets → Run again
commands.does: Writes 1, 3 and 5 to Link: the board asks the central for a 7.5–15 ms interval, the 2M PHY and 251-byte radio packets.
commands.fix: No change: the central decides. macOS often keeps 15 ms and allows 2M; some phones refuse 7.5 ms or 2M. That is the lesson: the peripheral can only ask.
commands.see: - new params: 15.00 ms …, - PHY now 2M / 2M; the next run is faster. The board's speed view keeps one bar per run with MTU, interval and PHY.

commands.command: pnpm tunnel → open the https address on your phone
commands.does: A cloudflared quick tunnel gives the app an https://…trycloudflare.com address, because phones only allow Web Bluetooth on https.
commands.fix: Bluefy says the page isn't secure: use the https address, not http.
commands.see: Android: Chrome opens it and the same chooser appears. iPhone: open it in the free Bluefy browser (Safari has no Web Bluetooth).

B5.goal: nRF Connect is a screwdriver; now you build the tool. esp-labs/apps/ble-app is a small React app that uses Web Bluetooth: the browser itself becomes the GATT client, so a web page on your Mac or phone talks to the board with no Wi-Fi, no server and no app store. The firmware keeps B3's Bench service and adds four characteristics: a Canvas you draw on from the phone, Sensors that stream five times a second, a Speed test that pushes notifications as fast as the radio allows, and Link controls to change the connection while you watch the speed move.
goalCheck: The app's Connect tab lists the Bench service with LED … Uptime plus Canvas, Sensors, Speed and Link (ba5e0010-0013), and its byte log shows every operation.
A stroke drawn in the Sketch tab appears on the board's sketch view within a fraction of a second.
The Live tab charts four lines; touching a jumper wire on GPIO 1 makes the touch line jump.
A 50 kB speed run ends with a kB/s figure in the app and the same run as a bar on the board's speed view; after Fast interval or 2M PHY the next run is visibly faster (or you can say why not).
B5.goalLine: Control and draw on the board from a web page, and measure how many bytes per second your link really carries.
B5.heading: Your own app, straight to the board
B5.note: Still no pairing: anyone near can connect, draw and read the sensors. B4's lock works the same here if you combine them. The app only ever sees boards you pick in the browser's chooser, and the browser hides some standard services from web pages on purpose. iPhones and Macs cache a device's GATT table by its address: if the explorer shows B3's old rows, turn Bluetooth off and on. Throughput depends mostly on the central: the same board is often 2-4× faster with a Mac than with a phone.

panels.intro: What happens between navigator.bluetooth.requestDevice() in the app and the LED changing colour, and how a notification finds its way back into a chart. Each step shows the real call or the real bytes on air. Pick a flow, then step with ◀ ▶.
panels.title: One colour change, from JavaScript to the LED

panels.intro: Throughput is decided by four numbers: how big each packet may be (MTU), how often the two radios meet (the connection interval), how many packets fit in one meeting, and how fast the bits fly (PHY). Move the sliders: the timeline shows three connection events with every packet drawn to scale, and the result is the same formula the Speed tab measures.
panels.title: How fast can it go?

panels.intro: Six views. Click for the next one; double-click on sketch clears it, on speed it starts a 50 kB run, on gatt it sends a Button click. Every gesture also reaches the app as a Button notification, as in B3.
panels.title: What the screen shows

steps: Same wiring as B1 (screen, button optional). Optional: one jumper wire in GPIO 1, free end loose: your touch sensor.
Flash ble-lab-b5. Checkpoint 1: the sketch view and the advertising rings.
Start the app (pnpm install once, then pnpm dev), open http://localhost:5177 in Chrome and Connect to Bench B5. Checkpoint 2: the GATT explorer lists nine Bench characteristics.
Colour wheel, message, then draw something in Sketch. Checkpoint 3: your drawing is on the board.
Open Live and touch the wire. Checkpoint 4: the touch line jumps in the app and on the board.
Speed: run 50 kB, then Fast interval + 2M PHY + Long packets and run again. Checkpoint 5: two bars; write down both kB/s figures and the interval each run used.
Optional: pnpm tunnel and repeat from your phone (Chrome on Android, Bluefy on iPhone). Compare its speed with the Mac's.
B5.title: Phone app

B6.cmd: uv run pio run -d labs/ble-lab-b6 -e ble-lab-b6 -t upload

commands.command: uv run pio run -d labs/ble-lab-b6 -e ble-lab-b6 -t upload
commands.does: Builds lab B6 and flashes it (no new downloads: NimBLE came with B1).
commands.fix: “Failed to connect”: hold BOOT, tap RST, release BOOT, run it again.
commands.see: ble-lab-b6: NimBLE 2.5.1 up, advertising as keyboard "Bench B6", the command list. The screen opens on the media view: “pair me: Bluetooth settings > Bench B6”.

commands.command: Bluetooth settings → Bench B6 → Connect / Pair
commands.does: Your phone or Mac connects, reads the Report Map, asks to pair (HID needs encryption), and stores a bond so it reconnects by itself next time.
commands.fix: Listed but won't connect: forget here AND “Forget This Device” on the phone, then pair again. A bond kept on only one side is the usual cause.
commands.see: + connected, then + secured: Just Works, bonded, key 16 B. The status bar shows the linked rings, a violet lock and a key. A Mac may open the Keyboard Setup Assistant: close it, or press the key it asks for and pick ISO (German) or ANSI (US).

commands.does: Start music on the phone (to its speaker, earbuds or your JBL). Click = play/pause, double-click = next track, hold under 2 s = mute, touch the wire on GPIO 2 / 1 (after touch on) = volume up / down.
commands.fix: Nothing happens? The app must have audio focus: play something first. On a Mac, Music/Spotify react; a browser tab may not.
commands.see: The icon ripples, a dot runs board → phone → speaker, and the music reacts. The monitor prints > media key: play/pause (usage 0CD).

commands.does: Open Notes (or any text field) on the paired device, then type this in the monitor. The board queues 2 reports per character (press, release) and sends 6 per frame, 8 ms apart.
commands.fix: Only the line says not paired yet? Pair first. Letters come out wrong: see layout.
commands.see: “hello bench” appears on the phone or Mac. The typer view fills its progress bar, then says typed 11 keys.

commands.does: Tells the board which layout the COMPUTER is set to, so it picks the right key for each character. Saved in NVS.
commands.fix: Still y/z swapped: the computer's layout is the other one. Check the input menu in the Mac's menu bar.
commands.see: layout German (QWERTZ) (saved). Now type yes gives “yes” on a German Mac. Characters the layout needs AltGr/Option for (@ [ ] { } \ | ~) are skipped with a warning.

commands.does: One key or a combo: modifiers (cmd, ctrl, alt, shift) plus a key (enter, tab, esc, arrows, f1-f12, a letter).
commands.fix: Windows: key win+r opens Run, key ctrl+alt+delete the security screen.
commands.see: Spotlight opens on the Mac (on an iPhone with a keyboard, the search too). The keys view shows modifier byte 08 (left GUI) and key 2C (space).

commands.does: Saves a text in NVS; a double-click on the typer view (or snippet alone) types it. A tiny macro pad.
commands.see: snippet saved, and the text on the typer view.

commands.does: Open a presentation (Keynote, PowerPoint, Google Slides in present mode). Click = right arrow (next), double-click = left arrow, hold under 2 s = b (black screen).
commands.see: The slide on the screen slides in from the side you moved to; the deck on the computer follows.

commands.does: The last reports, byte by byte: the modifier bits, the key numbers, and what each press types with the board's layout.
commands.see: down mod 02 key 04 types 'A' then up all zero for a capital A.

B6.goal: The board becomes a real Bluetooth keyboard: the same HID service every wireless keyboard has, so phones, Macs and PCs use it with their own driver. Its button turns into a remote: play/pause and skip the music on your phone (which can be playing on your JBL speaker), change the volume, click through slides, or type text you send from the serial monitor. You write the Report Map that tells the computer what our bytes mean, and you see why a keyboard never sends letters, only key numbers.
goalCheck: Your phone or Mac lists Bench B6 as a connected keyboard, and the screen's status bar shows the lock (encrypted) and the key (bonded).
A click on the media view pauses and resumes your music; a double-click skips the track; touching GPIO 2 turns it up.
type yes types “yes”, not “zes”: layout matches the computer's keyboard setting.
On the keys view you can read a press as bytes: modifier bits, key number, and the all-zero release after it.
B6.goalLine: Pair the board as a keyboard, control your music with the button, and type text in the right layout.
B6.heading: A Bluetooth keyboard and a remote for your music
B6.note: While an iPhone or iPad is connected to a hardware keyboard, its on-screen keyboard hides: disconnect the board (or switch Bluetooth off) to get it back. To unpair, forget the board on both sides (forget here, “Forget This Device” there). The ESP32-S3 has Bluetooth LE only: it can't stream audio to a speaker or headphones (that's Classic Bluetooth, A2DP), so the board controls the phone and the phone plays to your JBL. Volume and track keys go to whichever app has audio focus. Hosts disagree on what Option/AltGr characters live where, so the German table only types what it can type the same way on Mac and Windows.

panels.intro: Type in the box or press a key below and follow it: the board turns the character into a key number with ITS layout setting, sends 8 bytes, and the computer turns the number back into a character with ITS layout. Set the two layouts differently and type yes: that's the bug layout de fixes.
panels.title: A key press, from button to letter

panels.intro: Your JBL plays music over Classic Bluetooth audio. The ESP32-S3 only has Bluetooth LE, so it can't stream to it, but it can be the remote for the phone that does. Press a media key to follow it, or try the direct path to see where it fails.
panels.title: Why the board can't play to your speaker

panels.intro: Six views. Media and slides are modes: there the button is the remote (click, double-click, hold), and a 2-second hold moves on. On the other views a click moves on as usual.
panels.title: What the screen shows

steps: Same screen wiring. Optional: two jumper wires in GPIO 1 and GPIO 2 with the other ends loose (touch keys for volume). Flash ble-lab-b6.
On your phone or Mac, open Bluetooth settings and pair Bench B6. Checkpoint 1: lock and key in the status bar, secured: Just Works, bonded in the monitor.
Play music on the phone (to your JBL if you like). On the media view: click, double-click. Checkpoint 2: the music pauses, resumes and skips.
Type touch on (hands off the wires), then touch the GPIO 2 wire. Checkpoint 3: the volume goes up.
Open Notes, set layout to match the computer, and type yes, this is the bench. Checkpoint 4: exactly that text appears.
Hold the button 2 s to reach slides, open a presentation, click through it.
Click to the keys view and read one press: modifier bits, key number, then the release.
B6.title: Keyboard & media

B7.cmd: uv run pio run -d labs/ble-lab-b7 -e ble-lab-b7 -t upload

commands.command: uv run pio run -d labs/ble-lab-b7 -e ble-lab-b7 -t upload
commands.does: Builds lab B7 and flashes it.
commands.fix: “Failed to connect”: hold BOOT, tap RST, release BOOT, run it again.
commands.see: advertising as MIDI instrument "Bench B7", the command list, the keys view with five keys and a piano strip.

commands.command: Mac: Audio MIDI Setup → Window → Show MIDI Studio → Bluetooth icon → Bench B7 → Connect
commands.does: macOS connects to the board as a MIDI device (it may ask to pair: accept). Then open GarageBand with a software instrument: it hears every MIDI device.
commands.fix: iPhone/iPad: GarageBand → open a keyboard → settings (gear) → Advanced → Bluetooth MIDI Devices → Bench B7. Android: a BLE-MIDI app (e.g. “MIDI BLE Connect”) plus any synth. Chrome: the ble-app Music tab.
commands.see: + connected, asked for a 7.5-15 ms interval (low latency), + a synth is listening (subscribed). The keys view says “synth listening”.

commands.does: Plays the next note of the scale (300 ms). Double-click = a chord. Hold under 2 s = all notes off.
commands.fix: No sound but “synth listening”: in GarageBand, pick a software instrument track (not audio) and turn the volume up.
commands.see: A sound from GarageBand; the key lights violet on the piano strip; the roll draws a violet bar.

commands.does: Schedules a whole public-domain tune at the current tempo. loop() sends each note when it's due.
commands.see: tune twinkle: 14 notes, 8.4 s and the tune from the synth.

commands.does: The drum machine: 4 drums x 16 steps on MIDI channel 10, where General MIDI keeps the drums (36 kick, 38 snare, 42 hi-hat, 39 clap).
commands.fix: Drums sound like piano notes: the track's instrument isn't a drum kit.
commands.see: The sequencer view's playhead walks the grid; GarageBand plays drums (pick a drum kit track for the real sound).

commands.does: Five jumper wires on GPIO 1, 2, 6, 13, 14 (loose ends) become keys of the pentatonic scale. Hands off while it measures the baseline.
commands.fix: GPIO 13 and 14 are the RC522's wires from the RFID track: unplug the reader, or use the first three keys.
commands.see: touch on: 5 keys, pentatonic from C4; touching a wire end lights its key and plays the note, a firmer touch = louder.

commands.does: GarageBand (or the ble-app piano) sends MIDI back to the board as writes.
commands.fix: On a Mac, GarageBand doesn't send to MIDI devices: use the ble-app piano, or a DAW with MIDI output.
commands.see: Blue keys on the piano strip, blue bars on the roll, the LED in the note's colour, < note E4 vel 96 ch 1 lines.

commands.does: Explains the latency: notes wait for the next connection event.
commands.see: Your interval (7.5-15 ms if the host agreed, often 11.25 or 15 on Apple devices) and a press dropping to the next tick.

B7.goal: The board becomes a MIDI instrument over Bluetooth LE, using the standard BLE-MIDI service that GarageBand, Audio MIDI Setup, Android synth apps and Chrome all understand. MIDI carries notes, not sound: the synth on the other side makes the sound (and can send it to your JBL). Play with the button, five touch wires, serial commands and a 16-step drum machine; notes played on the other side light the board's piano strip and its LED. You see how notes are packed with timestamps, and why the connection interval sets the latency.
goalCheck: GarageBand (or the ble-app Music tab) lists Bench B7 and makes a sound when you click the button.
tune twinkle plays the tune; beat house + seq on plays drums on channel 10.
Notes you play on the synth's keyboard light the board's piano strip in blue, and the LED takes each note's colour.
The link view shows your connection interval, and you can say how long a note may wait for the radio.
B7.goalLine: Play notes from the board into a synth, and see the synth's notes on the board.
B7.heading: A Bluetooth MIDI instrument
B7.note: MIDI is instructions, not audio: the board never makes a sound itself (it has no speaker). The synth's audio can go anywhere it can play, your JBL included, through the phone or Mac's own Bluetooth. Apple hosts usually grant 11.25-15 ms connection intervals for MIDI, so a note waits up to one interval; the timestamps inside each packet let a good synth keep the rhythm anyway. If the Mac asks to pair, accept: the board allows Just Works bonding. Only public-domain tunes are built in.

panels.intro: Play the little keyboard (click, or the keys A to K on your computer). Notes pressed within one connection event share one packet. Watch the header, the timestamps, the status byte and running status, the trick that drops repeated status bytes.
panels.title: One note, byte by byte

panels.intro: A connected device may only talk at connection events, one every interval. Pick an interval and play: each note waits for the next event. Then compare a synth that plays notes when they arrive with one that uses the timestamps.
panels.title: Why notes wait: the connection interval

panels.intro: Five views. On keys, sequencer and roll the button is the instrument (click a note, double-click a chord or start/stop the drums, hold for all notes off, hold 2 s to move on).
panels.title: What the screen shows

steps: Same screen wiring. Optional: five jumper wires in GPIO 1, 2, 6, 13, 14 (unplug the RC522 first). Flash ble-lab-b7.
Connect from GarageBand (iPhone/iPad), Audio MIDI Setup + GarageBand (Mac), a BLE-MIDI app (Android) or the ble-app Music tab (Chrome). Checkpoint 1: “synth listening” on the keys view.
Click the button a few times, then double-click. Checkpoint 2: notes and a chord from the synth.
tune ode, then beat funk and seq on. Checkpoint 3: a tune and a drum groove.
Play the synth's keyboard. Checkpoint 4: blue keys and a coloured LED on the board.
Open the link view and read your interval. Try bpm 200 with the drums and listen: does it still feel tight?
B7.title: Music

B8.cmd: uv run pio run -d labs/ble-lab-b8 -e ble-lab-b8 -t upload

commands.command: uv run pio run -d labs/ble-lab-b8 -e ble-lab-b8 -t upload
commands.does: Builds lab B8 and writes it to the board. NimBLE-Arduino is already downloaded (B1).
commands.fix: “Failed to connect”: hold BOOT, tap RST, release BOOT, run it again.
commands.see: ble-lab-b8: NimBLE 2.5.1 up, address …, the command list, and the devices view filling up.

commands.does: Opens the serial monitor (and restarts the board).
commands.see: Bluetooth lab B8 Host (ble-lab-b8) and the commands.

commands.command: put the keyboard in pairing mode
commands.does: A keyboard already paired to your Mac only talks to the Mac. Pairing mode makes it advertise to anyone: usually hold the Bluetooth or channel key 3 s until its light blinks fast. Multi-channel keyboards: pick a channel your Mac isn't using.
commands.fix: Not there: it is still connected to the Mac (switch channel, or remove it in the Mac's Bluetooth settings). Apple Magic Keyboards use Classic Bluetooth and never show up here.
commands.see: The devices view: your keyboard near the top with a keyboard icon and HID.

commands.does: Prints the connectable devices, strongest first. Beacons are left out: they can't be connected to.
commands.see: 1 -48 dBm keyboard/mouse C4:7D:2A:91:0E:33 Bench Keys [HID]

commands.does: Sends CONNECT_IND to device 1 (now the board chooses the connection timing), then explores: discovers every service, characteristic and descriptor and reads the public basics.
commands.fix: no answer from …: it stopped advertising (pairing mode times out after ~60 s): start it again.
commands.see: > CONNECT_IND to Bench Keys, + connected: we are the central, + 5 services, 19 characteristics in 820 ms, - it is a keyboard/mouse (1812): type host. The explore view shows the tree; HID values say “locked until paired”.

commands.does: Pairs (bond + passkey + Secure Connections), reads the Report Map, finds each input report through its 2908 descriptor and subscribes (writes 01 00 into its CCCD).
commands.fix: pairing failed: the keyboard left pairing mode, or it still has an old bond with the board: forget, remove it on the keyboard side (pairing mode again), connect, host.
commands.see: Six big digits on the screen and ! type 482915 on the keyboard, then Enter. Type them on the keyboard, press Enter: + secured: passkey, bonded, key 16 B, < Report Map: 72 bytes, 11 input fields, > CCCD 01 00: report 1 (keyboard), + hosting: keyboard media keys. The view jumps to keyboard.

commands.does: Each key press is a notification: the board compares it with the previous one and adds the newly pressed keys. Backspace deletes, Enter starts a new line, Esc clears.
commands.fix: Wrong letters (y and z swapped)? See the next command.
commands.see: Your text on the keyboard view with a blinking cursor; the modifier caps light amber while you hold Shift, Ctrl, Alt or Cmd; the media keys show a violet toast.

commands.does: Key codes are positions, not letters. The board turns them into characters with the layout you choose: US or German.
commands.see: - layout German (QWERTZ): the same keys, other letters. Now the key printed Z gives z, and ä ö ü ß appear.

commands.does: The raw input reports, newest at the bottom, each byte coloured by the Report Map field it belongs to.
commands.see: #1 kbd 02 00 0B 00 00 00 00 00 with 02 amber (Left Shift) and 0B teal (the H key), and the decoded line under it.

commands.does: Boot protocol: the fixed 8-byte format every BIOS understands, without reading the Report Map. Compare with report protocol.
commands.fix: no Protocol Mode: this device has no boot mode: some keyboards don't offer it.
commands.see: > CCCD 01 00: report 0 (boot keyboard) and bootK rows on the reports view. boot off switches back.

commands.command: disconnect, then the mouse: pairing mode, connect <n>, long press
commands.does: A mouse has no keys and no screen, so pairing falls back to Just Works (no digits). Its Report Map describes buttons, X, Y and the wheel with whatever bit sizes it likes.
commands.fix: The cursor races across: that mouse reports in large steps; the board already halves them.
commands.see: + secured: Just Works, bonded, + hosting: mouse, and the mouse view: left button draws, right changes colour, middle clears, the wheel sets the brush.

commands.does: The bond (keys) is saved in NVS. When the keyboard advertises again (press a key to wake it), the board recognises its address and reconnects.
commands.fix: Keyboards that hide behind a changing private address (RPA) may not be recognised: connect + host by hand then.
commands.see: + bonded Bench Keys is back: reconnecting, then + secured: … with no passkey, and + hosting.

commands.does: Explore a device that isn't a keyboard. Only the public basics are read, nothing is written.
commands.fix: Not in the list: it only advertises BLE while the JBL app is looking, or right after power-on.
commands.see: A few services, mostly one long vendor UUID, and - JBL app's own service only: audio uses Classic BT. The audio itself never goes over BLE on this speaker, and this chip has no Classic Bluetooth.

commands.does: Deletes every bond on the board.
commands.see: - every bond deleted: pair again to use a keyboard. Remove the board on the keyboard side too (pairing mode), or it will refuse the next pairing.

B8.goal: Until now a phone or a laptop was the central and the board answered. Here the board is the central, the way your laptop is. It finds connectable devices, connects, and explores their GATT tables (read-only: only the public basics like name, maker and battery). Then it hosts your own BLE keyboard and mouse: it pairs (the board shows a passkey, you type it on the keyboard), reads the keyboard's own description of its reports (the Report Map), subscribes, and turns the raw bytes into text and a paint cursor on the screen.
goalCheck: host ends with + hosting: keyboard media keys (or mouse), after you typed the passkey on the keyboard.
What you type appears on the keyboard view; Shift, Ctrl, Alt and Cmd light up while held; layout de swaps Y and Z and shows ä ö ü ß.
On the reports view you can name every coloured byte: modifiers (amber), key codes (teal), mouse X (blue), Y (violet), wheel (coral).
After a power cycle the board reconnects to the bonded keyboard by itself, no passkey.
B8.goalLine: Pair your BLE keyboard with the board, type on its screen, and understand every byte the keyboard sends.
B8.heading: Swap roles: your keyboard types onto the board

commands.command: uv run pio run -d labs/rfid-lab-r1 -e rfid-lab-r1 -t upload
commands.does: Builds lab R1's firmware and writes it to the board (no new downloads: it only uses the display libraries you already have).
commands.fix: “Failed to connect”: hold BOOT, tap RST, release BOOT, run it again.
commands.see: Hard resetting via RTS pin…. The screen starts on the card view: rings, “Hold a card or tag”.

commands.does: Opens the serial monitor. Opening it restarts the board, so you see the start-up lines.
commands.fix: 0x00: the chip isn't powered or MISO is stuck low: check 3.3V, GND, RST. 0xFF: nobody drives MISO: check MISO (18) and SDA (15).
commands.see: RC522 on SPI3: SS 15 SCK 16 MOSI 17 MISO 18 RST 14 IRQ 13 · 4 MHz then VersionReg 0x92: MFRC522 v2.0 and the command list.

commands.does: Reads VersionReg (37h) once more: the 2-byte transfer shown above, live.
commands.fix: It changes, or turns into 00h/FFh after you touched the reader = a loose wire. Press the RC522's header in or solder it, then reset.
commands.see: The same line as at start-up (0x92, or e.g. 0xB2: FM17522 (clone)). Run it a few times, and again after moving the card around: it must never change.

commands.does: Pulses the RST wire (a hard reset of the chip), sets it up again and reads VersionReg. The firmware also checks VersionReg by itself every 2 s and does this on its own when the chip goes quiet.
commands.fix: Still 00h/FFh: power off, press the header pins in (or solder them), check 3.3V, GND, MISO (18), SDA (15).
commands.see: hard reset: VersionReg 0x92 (or your clone's value). If the chip had gone quiet: chip back after a hard reset = it had hung; still 0x00 after a reset = a wire.

commands.does: The datasheet's digital self-test (section 16.1.1): resets the chip and has it compute a fixed 64-byte sequence. A genuine NXP chip (91h/92h) is compared with the datasheet's table. A clone has no table, so the test runs twice and the two runs are compared. Polling pauses while it runs, so the card can stay where it is.
commands.fix: self-test skipped: chip silent (0x00) = the chip wasn't answering before the test even started: a wire, see reset. ! marks = bytes that differ: re-seat SCK/MOSI/MISO and run again. doesn't run the self-test = some clones simply don't have it; loopback is the test that counts then.
commands.see: 4 rows of 16 bytes with no ! marks, then self-test passed: 64/64 bytes match (NXP) or self-test consistent: 2 runs, same 64 bytes (clone). The chip view says passed or consistent.

commands.does: Writes 64-byte patterns into the chip's FIFO and reads them back, 50 times: 3,200 bytes each way.
commands.fix: Any errors at 4 MHz = a bad contact on SCK, MOSI or MISO, or wires much longer than 20 cm.
commands.see: FIFO loopback: 0 of 3200 bytes wrong at 4 MHz in teal at the bottom right of the screen.

commands.does: Prints 15 registers with their bits and what they mean.
commands.fix: TxControlReg 80h = antenna off: the chip was reset without our set-up. Unplug and replug the board.
commands.see: VersionReg 92h, TxControlReg 83h (antenna on), RFCfgReg 40h (33 dB gain), TPrescalerReg A9h + TReloadReg 03 E8 (a 25 ms timer: 1,000 ticks of 25 µs).

commands.does: Optional peek at the edge lab: runs the bus at 20 MHz, twice the chip's rating, then back to the default.
commands.fix: Always finish with spi 4. The R6 edge lab measures this properly.
commands.see: Maybe a few wrong bytes at 20 MHz, maybe none: it depends on your wires. The chip view's SPI clock turns amber above 10.

R1.goal: Its own firmware (rfid-lab-r1; every RFID lab has its own) with our own driver in kit/lib/rfid-kit: no RFID library, so every byte is ours to see. Eight wires put the RC522 on the S3's second SPI bus, so it never shares with the screen. The first conversation is with the chip itself, not a card: its version register, the self-test from the datasheet, and 3,200 bytes through its FIFO and back.
goalCheck: The monitor says VersionReg 0x92: MFRC522 v2.0 (or 0x91, or a clone's value), not 0x00 or 0xFF.
selftest ends with self-test passed: 64/64 bytes match on a genuine NXP chip (91h/92h), or self-test consistent: 2 runs, same 64 bytes on a clone such as the FM17522 (88h/B2h).
loopback says 0 of 3200 bytes wrong.
On the chip view: the square glows teal and the bus counters keep climbing.
R1.goalLine: Prove that the ESP32 and the reader chip talk to each other reliably over SPI, before any card is involved. Keep the card and the tag away for now.
R1.heading: Wire the reader and talk to its chip
R1.note: The on-board RGB LED tells you what the reader sees: a bright green flash each time a card is read, steady green while one lies on the reader, red if the reader chip stops answering (a wire), off otherwise. Many RC522 boards come with the header loose: push-in pins lose contact, so solder it or press it in firmly. IRQ is optional: without it the firmware polls, and the chip view says “polling” (R6 compares both). The card's position doesn't change any of R1's results. But handling it near the reader is the moment loose header pins lose contact: if VersionReg turns 00h/FFh afterwards, the firmware notices within 2 s, tries a hard reset and tells you whether it was a hang or a wire.

panels.intro: Every command in this lesson is built from transfers like this one. It is what a logic analyser would show on the four SPI wires while the ESP32 reads one register: 16 clock ticks, two bytes. The first byte goes out on MOSI and says which register and read or write; during the second byte the chip answers on MISO. chip does exactly this with VersionReg. Use ◀ ▶ to step bit by bit, pick another register, or choose a fault to see what a loose wire turns the answer into: that is how you'll read 00h or FFh in your own monitor.

Check twice: the module's 3.3V goes to 3V3, never 5V. The MFRC522 runs on 2.5–3.6 V and its pins are not 5 V tolerant.
Flash, then open the monitor (the first two commands above). Checkpoint 1: VersionReg 0x92 (or 0x91, or a clone value).
Type selftest. Checkpoint 2: “passed” (NXP chip) or “consistent” (a clone).
Type loopback, then regs. Checkpoint 3: 0 bytes wrong, and the register values from the table.

Click to the chip view and compare it with “What the screen shows”: teal square, passed, 4 MHz, bus counters climbing. That's the goal. Lay the card on the reader for a second as a preview of R2: the on-board LED flashes bright green and stays green while it lies there.

commands.does: Both cards wake on the same WUPA. The poll resolves the collision and selects one of them.
commands.fix: Only one card found? Overlap them more: both must sit inside the antenna's loop.
commands.see: The card view shows one UID (always the same one) and an amber line: collision at bit 23 (your bit will differ).

commands.command: inventory (or double-click on the card view)
commands.does: Switches the field off for 10 ms so every card restarts, then REQA → select → halt, again and again until nobody answers.
commands.fix: select failed (collision): move the cards a little and run it again.
commands.see: #1 9C:4F:6A:0D … collision at level 1 bit 23 -> chose 1, #2 9C:4F:2A:1B …, then inventory: 2 cards in the field.

commands.command: inventory with one card, then none
commands.does: Same walk, nothing to resolve.
commands.see: 1 card without a collision line, then 0 cards.

R3.goal: Lay the card and the tag on the reader together. Both answer at the same instant, bit by bit, and where their UIDs differ the reader hears a collision. Anticollision walks down the bits like a binary tree: pick a branch, ask again with that prefix, select the card that's left, halt it, repeat until nobody answers.
goalCheck: inventory lists 2 cards with both UIDs.
It names the collision bit, and the walk-through above lands on the same bit with your two UIDs.
R3.goalLine: Find both cards at once, and point to the exact bit where their UIDs collided.
R3.heading: Two cards at once: anticollision
R3.note: Bits travel least-significant first, so “bit 23” is bit 6 of the third UID byte. Our driver is tested for two cards at once: with three or more, the chip's collision position after the first branch is harder to trust. 7-byte UIDs take two cascade levels; the first part starts with 88h, the cascade tag.

panels.intro: The two rows are the UID bits of two cards, in the order they travel (least significant bit of byte 0 first). Step through: where the bits differ the reader hears a collision, picks 1, and only the matching card keeps answering. Type your own UIDs from the monitor.

R4.goal: A MIFARE Classic 1K holds 1,024 bytes: 16 sectors × 4 blocks × 16 bytes. Every sector has its own lock, the trailer: two keys plus access bits that say who may read or write each block. Open each sector of your own card with the factory key and dump it.
goalCheck: dump ends with dump: 16 sectors read, and the memory view is all coloured (no grey “closed” sectors).
In the dump you can point to the UID in block 0 and to FF 07 80 69 in a trailer, and the decoder above explains what FF 07 80 allows.
R4.goalLine: Dump your own card's whole memory and explain block 0 and one sector trailer byte by byte.

R4.note: Authentication runs inside the MFRC522 (its MFAuthent command): the ESP32 hands over the key and never sees the handshake, and the key never goes into the trace. The firmware only uses the factory key, on cards you own, and never writes block 0 or a trailer: a trailer with broken access bits locks its sector for good.

R7.goal: Its own firmware (rfid-lab-r7) turns the bench into a door you manage from a small React app (esp-labs/apps/door-app) over your Wi-Fi. The board keeps the card list in its flash and decides every tap itself; the card only brings its UID. From the app you add cards, name them, give them a role, block them, limit them to hours, an end date or a number of uses, copy one card's rules to another, replace a lost card, write a name label onto them, wipe the data the labs wrote, save a card's data and write it back or copy it onto another card, open the door remotely, switch on lockdown, and watch every tap live. Two simulated locks (the screen and the LED): the front door, for every role, and the admin room, for admin cards only; the one reader is mounted at one of them at a time.
goalCheck: The app shows live and both tags are in the list: the white card as a resident, the key tag as a guest.
Tapping the white card shows OPEN on the screen and in the app; after Block the same tap shows DENIED · blocked.
The guest tag's uses go down with each tap; at 0 it is refused with “no uses left”.
Every tap and every change appears in the access log, on the board's log view and in the app.
The white card's data is saved, copied onto the key tag and compared: same data, and the key tag still opens as Key tag, because a copy never moves the UID.
R7.goalLine: Run your two tags as a small access system: one resident, one guest, and see each rule decide a tap.

R7.note: Why the board decides and not the card: a card's UID and the data on a MIFARE Classic can be read by anyone with a reader, so they are fine as a name tag, not as proof. Real access systems keep the decision on a server and use cards with modern cryptography (e.g. MIFARE DESFire); this lab teaches the server side of that. Reading the API is open on your Wi-Fi; every change needs the token. The card list lives in the board's NVS and survives re-flashing; it is separate from the R1-R6 labs. Copying moves data only: block 0 is written once at the factory, so the copy keeps its own UID and the door treats it as a different card. That is also why access never rests on the data: it would be copied along.

S1.goal: KY-037 or INMP441Two microphones, two ways in. The INMP441 is digital: its own amplifier and 24-bit converter, numbers over I2S. The KY-037 has two outputs. AO is the microphone's own voltage: a tiny wave riding on a steady bias. DO is a yes/no from the LM393 comparator, set by the blue trim pot. S1 samples AO 16 000 times a second with the ADC's DMA (no analogRead() in a loop), draws it as an oscilloscope, shows where it sits in the ADC's range, and lets you tune the pot. The mics view puts both side by side. Every other sound lab stands on this: the sampler, the 4-second ring and the level meter live in kit/lib/sound-kit.
goalCheck: The scope shows a flat line while you're quiet and a wave when you talk; a whistle stands still (trigger on).
The bias view shows your module's bias in mV and no CLIPPING when you clap close to it; you tried atten 6 and saw the step size halve.
On the comparator view, DO lights with claps and stays dark while you talk normally: “tuned”.
status says 16000 Hz measured and DMA overruns 0.
With both mics wired, the mics view says how many dB more clearly the INMP441 hears a word.
S1.goalLine: See your voice and a clap as a wave, compare the two microphones, read the bias (or the bits), and tune the comparator so it fires only with loud sounds.
S1.heading: Hear what the microphones really send
S1.note: With the INMP441 the scope's scale is in % of full scale, the bias view becomes a ladder of its 24 bits (each bit = 6 dB; how many the sound uses, the headroom left), the comparator is software, and numbers adds dB SPL. Honest expectations for the KY-037: it has no amplifier. Its AO is the capsule's raw voltage, a few millivolts for a voice, so speech uses only a handful of the ADC's 4096 steps. That makes it a good loudness sensor (claps, knocks, noise, beats) and only a rough microphone. DO is a single comparator: a clap makes dozens of edges on it as the wave crosses the line, so the labs listen to AO and use DO for the hardware lamp and as a second opinion. The ADC samples through ADC1, which keeps working while Wi-Fi is on (ADC2 doesn't).

head: Module pin
ESP32-S3
Notes
rows: The analog mic. + on the second 3V3 pin (the screen has the first), G on GND. Never 5 V: AO and DO swing up to the module's supply, and the ESP32-S3's pins take 3.3 V at most.
Analog out: the microphone's voltage. GPIO 6 is ADC1 channel 5: ADC1 keeps working while Wi-Fi is on, ADC2 doesn't.
Digital out: the LM393 comparator says high when the sound is louder than the blue trim pot's setting.
The digital mic (I2S). VDD on 3V3 (share the breadboard rail with the KY-037), GND on GND. 3.3 V only.
Low = it talks in the left slot, the one the board reads.
The bit clock. The ESP32 drives it: 16 000 × 64 = 1.024 MHz.
Word select: left slot / right slot, flips every 32 clock ticks.
The data, most significant bit first. Pulled down, so a missing mic reads as zeros.
The speaker amplifier. 5V gives the most (about 3 W into 4 Ω); 3V3 works, quieter.
Bit clock of the second I2S port (I2S1; the mic uses I2S0, so both run at once).
Leave both unconnected: 9 dB gain, and it plays (left + right) / 2.
On the amplifier's screw terminal: the JST-PH2.0 lead's two wires, red to +.
Unchanged. The push button on GPIO 5 is optional: it does what BOOT does.

S2.goal: KY-037 or INMP441MAX98357A + speaker (optional)How loud is it? With the INMP441 S2 shows real dB SPL (its datasheet says −26 dBFS at 94 dB SPL, so RMS dBFS + 111): 30 whisper, 60 talk, 85 the hearing-risk line. With the KY-037 it shows dB above your room's quiet. S2 turns the samples into decibels the way a sound level meter does: fast (125 ms) or slow (1 s) smoothing, a peak hold, and a noise floor that learns your room. Then it keeps a minute of graph, a ten-minute noise diary, and an alarm that lights lesson 02's LED on GPIO 4 when it stays too loud.

S2.note: dB SPL needs a microphone whose sensitivity is known: the INMP441's is in its datasheet, so S2 can show it (unweighted, about ±2 dB; real meters often show dBA, which weights the frequencies like the ear and reads lower for a deep hum). S7.goal: MAX98357A + speakerNumbers go out over I2S to the MAX98357A, a class-D amplifier: it switches the speaker fully on and off about 300 000 times a second, and how long each pulse lasts follows the number. The cone is too slow to follow, so it moves with the average: the wave. S7 makes notes in five timbres, chords, envelopes, tunes and game sounds, and draws what you hear.
goalCheck: beep and the hello chime come out of the speaker at vol 20.
On wave, the spectrum shows one line for sine, odd harmonics for square, all for saw.

S7.goalLine: Hear the difference between the five waves, play a chord and a tune, change the envelope until a note plucks, and fire every game sound.
S7.heading: Make the board play: a synth on one speaker
S7.note: One speaker, one stream: chords and tunes are rendered into PSRAM first (up to 30 s), then played. At 16 000 samples a second nothing above 8 kHz exists, so a square or saw's high harmonics fold back down as wrong frequencies: a slight grit on high notes, the honest limit of a simple synth. Every other sound lab uses the same speaker for its chimes, and the echo guard keeps its detectors deaf while it plays.

Say something and the parrot says it back: normal, as a chipmunk (1.5× faster), a giant (0.7×), a robot (ring modulator + 6-bit crunch), with an echo, or reverse. Then live effects: an echo you talk into, a robot voice. The parrot is voice-activated like S4 (12 dB, 0.3 s pre-roll, 0.7 s hold, 6 s at most) and never hears itself.

You provoked (and the guard stopped) a howl by pointing the speaker at the mic: Howl! Move the speaker away or turn it down.
S8.goalLine: Make the parrot repeat you in three voices, talk through the live echo without a howl, and explain why a chipmunk talks fast.
S8.heading: A parrot that repeats you, and a live robot voice
S8.note: Changing the speed of a recording changes its pitch and its length together: that's why the chipmunk talks fast. Keeping the speed while shifting the pitch needs much more DSP (grains or a phase vocoder). Feedback: if what the mic hears comes back louder than it went out (loop gain above 1), it goes round and round: the howl. The guard cuts the live effect when the level keeps climbing (9 dB within 300 ms) or stays above −12 dBFS. Latency = one screen frame of processing + the speaker's queue + its 16 ms DMA block.
